analysis.one_liner: Lets Americans aged 55 to 64 buy into Medicare by paying premiums that cover the cost.
analysis.headline: Backed by 22 Senate Democrats, the bill died in the Senate Finance Committee without ever getting a vote.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would create a new Medicare option for people aged 55 to 64 — the years before most Americans qualify for Medicare at 65. Anyone in that age band who is not already eligible for Medicare could enroll and receive full hospital, medical, and prescription drug benefits, including the option to join a Medicare Advantage plan. Enrollees would pay a monthly premium calculated to cover the estimated per-person cost of their care, so the buy-in is designed to be self-financing rather than a new taxpayer expense. The bill also guarantees that enrollees can buy supplemental 'Medigap' policies and lets them count the coverage toward Affordable Care Act subsidies.
analysis.who_benefits: Americans aged 55 to 64 who lack affordable coverage — especially early retirees, workers whose employers dropped coverage, and people priced out of the individual market — could buy into Medicare with full hospital, medical, and drug benefits. The bill guarantees them access to Medigap supplemental policies at first enrollment and each time they re-enroll, something many states do not require in that age band. It also treats the buy-in coverage as a qualified health plan for ACA purposes, so lower-income enrollees could still receive premium and cost-sharing subsidies, and it bars any negative impact on existing Medicare beneficiaries or the Medicare trust funds.

how_it_helps.text: Every U.S. citizen or permanent resident aged 55 to 64 who is not otherwise Medicare-eligible could enroll and receive the same hospital, medical, and prescription drug benefits (and protections) as regular Medicare beneficiaries, including the choice of a Medicare Advantage plan [S3].

Monthly premiums would be set at one-twelfth of the estimated average annual per-person cost of benefits and administration for the buy-in population, and the collections would be deposited into the Medicare Hospital Insurance and Supplementary Medical Insurance Trust Funds, keeping the option self-financing by design [S3].

Enrollees would have a guaranteed right to buy Medigap supplemental policies at first enrollment and on each re-enrollment, and when they turn 65 they would be treated as new Medicare enrollees for Medigap purposes [S3].

Buy-in coverage would count as minimum essential coverage, be treated as a qualified health plan for ACA premium tax credits, and be treated as silver-level coverage for cost-sharing subsidies, with HHS treated as the plan's issuer [S2] [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Enrollees themselves would pay the full monthly premium, set to cover the average cost of their care, so the bill does not create a new general-taxpayer subsidy — though premiums in this age band, whose per-person costs are high, would likely be substantial. The Secretary is directed to implement the option with no effect on benefits for existing Medicare beneficiaries and no negative impact on the Medicare trust funds. The industries that bear the cost are private insurers and others who would have sold coverage to 55-to-64-year-olds and now lose some of that business to Medicare — though insurers could still capture those customers through Medicare Advantage plans, which the bill explicitly allows.

drawbacks.text: Enrollees would pay premiums equal to the full estimated per-person cost of care for their age band, and unlike most Medicare beneficiaries they would be ineligible for Medicaid help with Medicare cost-sharing, so out-of-pocket costs could still be heavy for lower-income participants [S2] [S3].

If the buy-in mainly attracted sicker 55-to-64-year-olds leaving ACA marketplaces, the marketplace risk pools could thin and premiums there could rise for people who stay; the bill counts buy-in coverage as silver-level for subsidy purposes but does not include a specific mechanism to offset such a shift [S3].

The bill forbids any negative impact on the Medicare trust funds and instructs the Secretary to implement it that way, but it does not spell out how to reconcile that requirement if actual per-person costs run above the premium estimates [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For the roughly ten-year stretch before Medicare eligibility, this offered a straightforward option: pay a premium covering your expected care costs and get Medicare's provider network, benefit rules, and guaranteed Medigap access. It was deliberately self-financing, which limits the risk to taxpayers but also means it offers no affordability rescue on its own — premiums for 55-to-64-year-olds would be high, and cost-sharing subsidies would flow only through the ACA, not Medicaid. The main honest concern is adverse selection: the design depends on enough healthier people joining to keep premiums near estimates. On balance a real coverage gain for a group that often falls through the cracks, with predictable but real limits.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the Senate Finance Committee the day it was introduced and the committee never took it up, so it died when that Congress ended.

narrative.text: Stabenow and seven fellow Democratic senators introduced the bill on August 3, 2017, and it was read twice and referred to the Committee on Finance [S5].
The cosponsor list grew to 21 Democratic senators, all from one party [S4].

No further action appears in the record: the Finance Committee never held a hearing or markup, the bill never reached the Senate floor, and no vote was ever held before the 115th Congress ended on January 3, 2019 [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Private insurers and others who would have competed with a Medicare buy-in for 55-to-64-year-olds kept that market unchanged. Americans in that age band without affordable coverage gained nothing, since the option was never enacted.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Private insurers who kept the 55-64 market

sides.party_line_note: All 22 Senate supporters were Democrats and no Republican cosponsored; with a Republican-held Senate and Finance Committee, the bill never advanced.

industries.note: Insurers selling individual and small-group coverage would have lost some 55-to-64-year-old customers to a Medicare option. The bill's failure leaves that market exactly as it was.

The bill lets 55-to-64-year-old enrollees choose Medicare Advantage plans, so insurers could still capture buy-in enrollees — and they would be paid Medicare rates for doing so. The plan the bill failed to pass would have partially entrenched, not displaced, their role.

The bill would have created a guaranteed-issue right to Medigap policies for every buy-in enrollee at 55 and on each re-enrollment, a new mandated sales opportunity — though a guaranteed-issue mandate also limits how these insurers can price or deny. The bill died, so nothing changed for them.

More insured 55-to-64-year-olds would mean fewer unpaid bills and more patients able to seek care; providers would have been paid under Medicare rates. Nothing changed because the bill never advanced.
